items.title: Biological Invasions and the Reconfiguration of Global Biogeographical Patterns
items.abstract: Aim Biological invasions are redistributing species across the planet, yet their consequences for the spatial patterns that structure biodiversity remain poorly resolved. Here, we synthesise empirical evidence to evaluate how human‐mediated species introductions are reshaping the core biogeographical rules that describe the geography of life on Earth. Location Global, covering terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems. Time Period Contemporary (20th–21st centuries), corresponding to the acceleration of biological invasions under globalisation. Major Taxa Studied Plants, vertebrates, and invertebrates; with additional evidence from other taxa where available. Methods We performed a systematic review of the literature across major biogeographical patterns, including latitudinal diversity gradients, biogeographical regionalisation, species–area and diversity–isolation relationships, Bergmann's and Rapoport's ecogeographical rules and range‐size distributions. Searches in Web of Science and Google Scholar identified 2652 records, of which 150 publications met inclusion criteria. Records were classified by ecological unit, taxon, ecosystem, spatial scale, outcome relative to rule expectations, effect pathway, and explanatory driver. Results Biological invasions are substantially altering global biodiversity patterns. Several long‐standing relationships, such as the delineation of global biogeographical regions, island diversity–isolation gradients, and Bergmann's Rule, are already fundamentally reshaped. Others, including species‐area relationships and range‐size distributions, are reinforced or remain consistent with classical expectations. Effects are strongest at broad spatial scales and in highly invaded systems, particularly islands and temperate regions. Across rules, outcomes were driven mainly by spatial variation in colonisation and propagule pressure, with additional relevant roles for environmental filtering and temporal dynamics. Main Conclusions Biological invasions are redefining the geography of life in the Anthropocene. While some biogeographical regularities persist, others are being weakened or replaced by novel human‐driven patterns. This selective reorganisation points to a shift from biogeography structured primarily by dispersal limitation, environmental filtering, and evolutionary history toward one increasingly shaped by anthropogenic transport, introduction history, and invasion pressure.

items.title: Anticipating conflict as large mammals return to Europe's changing countryside
items.abstract: Research Highlight: Bluhm, H., Kowalczyk, R., Klich, D., Olech, W., Perzanowski, K., Retez, G., Skorupski, J., Zurell, D., Tracz, M., Tracz, M., Baryło, R., Wołoszyn‐Gałęza, A., Januszczak, M., & Kuemmerle, T. (2026). Using individual‐based modelling to anticipate future conflict potential for expanding European bison populations. Journal of Applied Ecology , 63 (7), e70481. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365‐2664.70481 . Rural depopulation, legal protection and reintroduction have driven large mammal recovery in parts of Europe; however, escalating human–wildlife conflict constrains the extent of this recovery. Bluhm et al. integrated spatial indicators of crop damage, forestry damage and traffic collisions into an individual‐based population model to anticipate where conflict involving European bison ( Bison bonasus ) may arise over the next century across five Central European countries. The model projected a threefold increase in the bison population to 7580 individuals and continued range expansion. Conflict hotspots emerged in north‐eastern Poland (crop damage), western Poland (all conflict types) and western Germany (traffic). The study also identified three low‐conflict ‘coldspots’, unlikely to be colonised naturally, as candidate reintroduction sites. Regulating populations at low‐conflict densities reduced projected abundance by more than 35% and patch occupancy by nearly 50% over 100 years, whereas increased traffic mortality reduced abundance by approximately 10%. These results expose a trade‐off between reducing conflict and restoring the ecological functions of recovering megaherbivores. They favour protecting bison during recovery and deploying non‐lethal mitigation in predicted hotspots, and they point to the need for models that capture changing land use and social attitudes.

items.title: A Global Study Reveals a Stronger Temperature‐Cell Size Relationship in Diatoms on Islands Than on Continents
items.abstract: Aim To study (i) the differences in mean diatom community biovolume (MDCB) and proportion of large taxa (PLT) between insular and continental communities, (ii) their response to environmental and geographic factors and (iii) their latitudinal patterns. Location Africa, America, Europe and the Pacific. Time Period Present. Major Taxa Studied Stream diatoms. Methods We compared MDCB and PLT between islands and continents globally and in two of four study regions (America and Europe). Using random forest models, we assessed and compared the response of MDCB and PLT to environmental and geographic variables, the temperature‐MDCB and temperature‐PLT relationships and their latitudinal patterns in both islands and continents. Main Results The MDCB was significantly smaller on islands than on continents, although the difference was comparatively small. Mean temperature and temperature seasonality were the strongest determinants of MDCB and PLT in communities on islands and on continents at a global scale, whereas at a regional scale, their main drivers varied across regions and systems. Islands exhibited a stronger poleward increase of diatom biovolume compared to continents. Main Conclusions Mean diatom community biovolume decreased with mean temperature on both islands and continents globally, but temperature had a more prominent effect on islands than on continents. This supports the temperature‐size relationship for diatoms at a macroecological scale, especially on islands. Our results suggest that global warming may reduce the mean biovolume of diatom communities through the replacement of large species by small ones and that this reduction may occur at a faster rate on islands than on continents, with potentially profound effects on ecosystem functions.

items.title: Contrasting projections of environmental suitability across a breeding raptor assemblage under climate change
items.abstract: Climate change is altering species distributions globally, with potentially important consequences for predator communities and ecosystem functioning. Raptors may be particularly informative indicators of these changes, yet projections of future suitability remain uncertain. Here, I used maximum entropy species distribution models (MaxEnt) to quantify current and future environmental suitability for 16 breeding raptor species across the United Kingdom (UK), with future suitability projected under five global climate models (GCMs), two emissions scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), and two time periods (2041–2060 and 2061–2080). Spatially cross-validated model performance varied among species (mean AUC = 0.607–0.848; TSS = 0.077–0.563), with 13 of 16 species having mean TSS scores < 0.40. Projected responses to climate change were strongly species-dependent. Under the most pessimistic climatic scenario (SSP5-8.5 in 2061–2080), suitable area increased by 73.5 ± 17.0% (mean ± SD among GCMs) for Peregrine Falcon (Falco peregrinus) and 41.0 ± 15.6% for Hen Harrier (Circus cyaneus), although both species had relatively low TSS values. Contrastingly, all five GCMs projected declines in suitability for White-tailed Eagle (Haliaeetus albicilla), Short-eared Owl (Asio flammeus), Red Kite (Milvus milvus) and Merlin (Falco columbarius) under SSP5-8.5 (2061–2080), whereas the projected decline for Eurasian Goshawk (Astur gentilis) was less consistent among GCMs. White-tailed Eagle was predicted to experience the largest proportional decline (97.2 ± 6.1%), although this was relative to a small current suitable area of 2,306 km², while Short-eared Owl declined by 67.6 ± 29.5%. Spatial transition analyses revealed notable differences in persistence, decrease and increase in suitable areas among species. For Short-eared Owl and Red Kite, 78.5% and 43.4% of currently suitable area may become unsuitable under SSP5-8.5 in 2061–2080, respectively. Conversely, Peregrine Falcon retained all currently suitable area while increasing 82,833 km² of newly suitable area. Considerable between-GCM variation for some species highlights the importance of incorporating climate-model uncertainty alongside model performance when interpreting future projections. Breeding raptors in the UK are unlikely to response uniformly to climate change. Instead, these projections demonstrate contrasting patterns of persistence, increases and decreases in future environmental suitability. Conservation responses should be species-specific and must account for both projected change and associated uncertainty.

items.title: Conservation hotspots and marine protected areas: Revealing opportunities to protect threatened chondrichthyans in the North‐East Atlantic
items.abstract: Chondrichthyans (sharks, skates, rays and chimaeras) are among the most threatened marine vertebrates, yet their conservation in the North‐East Atlantic remains poorly addressed. Marine protected areas (MPAs) constitute key spatial conservation tools but their contribution to chondrichthyan conservation has not been systematically evaluated. We compiled a dataset of fisheries‐dependent and independent surveys (2009–2021) and applied hierarchical Bayesian joint species distribution models accounting for spatial autocorrelation and gear‐specific differences in detection. Forty‐one chondrichthyan species (18 continental shelf and 23 deep‐water), predominantly demersal, had sufficient occurrence data to model their distribution across the North‐East Atlantic. These distributions allowed us to identify conservation hotspots based on species richness and the proportion of IUCN Red List threatened species, with critical hotspots defined as those above the 95th percentile of both metrics. Conservation hotspots for continental shelf species covered more than twice the area of deep‐water species hotspots (67,152 and 31,180 km 2 , respectively). Overall, 32% of continental shelf species and 35% of deep‐water species conservation hotspot areas overlapped with existing MPAs. However, coverage differed markedly for critical hotspots, with 85% of critical deep‐water species hotspots coinciding with MPAs against 16% of critical continental shelf species hotspots. Most conservation hotspots overlapping MPAs occurred within sites whose designation included benthic habitats. As most modelled species were demersal, management measures targeting damaging activities such as bottom trawling in these areas could provide indirect conservation benefits for these chondrichthyans. This highlights a management lever to improve protection, even at sites not designated to protect these species. Synthesis and applications . Our results identify three complementary pathways for action: (i) targeted new or expanded area‐based conservation measures in unprotected conservation hotspots such as the central Celtic Sea; (ii) enhanced management within existing MPAs where they already overlap with conservation hotspots, including gear restrictions, bycatch mitigation and seasonal closures; and (iii) integration of complementary data sources to strengthen the evidence base for currently data‐limited species, particularly pelagic chondrichthyans. Together, these actions provide a spatial framework to guide where conservation measures may be most relevant and support more effective chondrichthyan conservation across the North‐East Atlantic.

items.title: Structural connectivity measures predict urban bird richness better than functional connectivity measures, even after controlling for habitat amount
items.abstract: Context Urban planning increasingly emphasizes landscape connectivity to mitigate biodiversity loss. However, across the many connectivity measures available, they are rarely validated against biological outcomes or disentangled from the independent effects of habitat amount, especially across spatial scales. Thus, the independent role of connectivity structuring biodiversity is unclear. Objectives Our objective was to evaluate how different types of connectivity metrics independently predict urban species richness after controlling for habitat availability. We aimed to quantify the strength and direction of the relationship between a set of connectivity metrics on urban avian richness. Methods We evaluated the relationship between bird species richness, based on 148,899 eBird checklists across 18 Canadian cities, and a set of connectivity metrics calculated with high-resolution land cover data using generalized additive models. We modelled checklist-level bird richness as a function of ten connectivity metrics spanning four categories, structural, graph‑network, potential, and functional connectivity. To disentangle the independent effect of the connectivity metrics, the models included habitat amount and sampling effort, across three spatial scales. Results Generalized additive models accounting for habitat amount, sampling effort, spatial autocorrelation, and city effects explained 30–33% of deviance in species richness, but connectivity metrics contributed relatively little independent explanatory power. Contrary to expectations, simple structural metrics describing greenspace aggregation and cohesion were positively associated with species richness, and consistently outperformed graph‑based, potential, and functional measures. However, connectivity effects weakened with increasing spatial scale. Conclusions Our results suggest that, for urban birds, landscape configuration influences richness primarily through habitat aggregation, supporting the use of simple structural metrics in urban conservation planning.

items.title: From turf to bare rock: the ecological footprint of an invasive urchin on fast-warming temperate reefs
items.abstract: Overgrazing of macrophytes is an increasing ecological threat to coastal ecosystems, that occurs due to overfishing of top predators and/or to rapid tropicalization of temperate systems. Tropicalization is driven mostly by range expansion or bioinvasion of tropical species assisted by ocean warming. The Mediterranean Sea is a global hotspot of tropicalization where tropical rabbitfish are already a major threat to marine forests in the eastern basin, turning forests into turf barrens. Recently, the expanding invasion of the sea urchin Diadema setosum may further increase this threat to Mediterranean reef ecosystems. In 2006, this invader coming from the Indo Pacific, the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, was discovered on the coasts of Turkey, and its populations have since expanded to both the eastern and southeastern Mediterranean. The arrival of D. setosum created a knowledge gap regarding its potential ecological impacts. The aim of this study was to test these impacts utilizing lab and field experiments. We used a mesocosm facility to test grazing rates on turf-covered boulders under ambient and elevated temperatures, and a caging experiment to test grazing impacts in the field. In both experiments, all or most rock algal cover was grazed within weeks, leaving bare rock. Increasing populations and grazing intensity of D. setosum is expected to further reduce rabbitfish turf barrens down to bare rock, as a shift-phase, reducing the contribution of these reefs to the ecosystem functionality even further. Results highlight the critical need for prompt implementation of D. setosum removal campaigns across the region.

items.abstract: Understanding the drivers of bee phenology is important for predicting how climate change may alter the temporal overlap between bee activity and plant flowering, with consequences for pollination. items.title: Reconciling multiple views of global marine plankton diversity
items.abstract: Marine plankton diversity influences key ecosystem properties, including primary production and carbon export, and is monitored using diverse observation systems. Yet, it remains unclear whether global diversity patterns from different observation streams converge, and whether potential commonalities can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation. Using a habitat modelling (CEPHALOPOD), we compare plankton diversity patterns across observation types and metrics, relating global open-ocean surface diversity from 330,000 observations of occurrence, abundance, biomass, and relative metagenomic reads to environmental climatologies. We find that diversity patterns converge on a latitudinal diversity gradient, with tropical oligotrophic gyres, western boundary currents and the Info-Pacific archipelago emerging as diversity hotspots. Occurrence-based estimates indicate higher diversity in eastern boundary upwellings than estimates accounting for community dominance, showing how multiple observation types provide complementary views of diversity. Surface ocean temperature, primary production, and physical transport emerge as remotely observable diversity proxies that can guide in situ sampling. Finally, diversity-ecosystem functioning relationships depend on the observation system: occurrence-based estimates highlight how diverse species can support production through complementary ecological roles, whereas abundance-, biomass-, and metagenomic-based estimates better reflect how dominant species contribute to processes such as carbon export. These findings can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation under climate change.

items.title: The Spatial Scaling of Species' Climatic Niche Geometry
items.abstract: Aim Climatic associations of species, particularly the geometry of their climatic niches (e.g., niche breadth and shape), are central ecological characteristics and key to robust assessment and forecasting of biodiversity. While climatic niches are known to depend on spatial grain, a consensus on the generality of this dependence and its underlying drivers remains elusive. Location Western Hemisphere. Time Period 1981–2018. Major Taxa Studied Birds (Aves). Methods We developed a quantitative framework to measure and predict the spatial scaling of species' realized climatic niche geometry. We examined variation in niche breadth and shape across a two‐order‐of‐magnitude grain size gradient (1–100 km) for 1810 bird species across the Western Hemisphere. We tested the hypotheses that the magnitude and slope of spatial scaling in niche geometry are primarily driven by three key factors: (1) geographic range size, (2) habitat specialization and (3) landscape environmental heterogeneity. We further evaluated whether readily available coarse‐grain data can reliably predict fine‐grain niche breadth using these spatial scaling relationships. Results We found that for a quarter of the studied species, realized niche breadths differed by at least twofold across the 1–100 km grain gradient. Species occupying environmentally heterogeneous landscapes, with restricted geographic ranges and specialized habitat requirements, showed greater sensitivity of niche geometry to spatial grain. Furthermore, when combined with species' ecological and geographical attributes, these spatial scaling relationships allow robust prediction of fine‐grain niche breadth using coarse‐grain data. Main Conclusions Our results show that the spatial scaling of climatic niche geometry differs substantially across species with divergent landscape and ecological attributes. Future niche‐based studies should explicitly account for grain‐dependence. When fine‐grain occurrence data are unavailable, cross‐grain data integration can effectively mitigate scale‐driven biases in niche estimates.

items.title: Trait‐based assessment of fire regime risk to threatened fauna
items.abstract: Fire regimes are rapidly changing worldwide, increasing extinction risk for many animal species and placing growing pressure on fire management to balance biodiversity conservation with other objectives. Effective fire planning requires an understanding of how different components of the fire regime (time since fire, fire frequency, and fire severity) interact to influence species persistence. However, species‐specific data are often sparse, context dependent, or unavailable at the scales required for decision‐making, limiting the capacity to assess biodiversity risk directly. Here, we develop a risk‐based framework for assessing animal vulnerability to fire regimes by grouping species into trait‐informed fire response groups (FRGs) that exhibit similar patterns of survival, recovery, and abundance following fire. Using structured expert elicitation supported by targeted literature synthesis, we estimated fire response curves for 94 threatened animal species across New South Wales, Australia. These curves describe relative abundance trajectories across gradients of time since fire, fire frequency, and fire severity, allowing comparison of how different elements of the fire regime exacerbate or mitigate risk. We identified 18 FRGs that were further synthesized into five broad fire response strategies (FRSs) capturing consistent patterns of resilience and vulnerability. Fire severity was positively associated with strong and relatively uniform declines in abundance across all groups, indicating limited tolerance to high‐severity fire regardless of other traits. In contrast, responses to time since fire and fire frequency varied markedly among FRGs. Species dependent on long‐unburnt habitats or slow‐recovering resources were disproportionately vulnerable to frequent fire, while some generalist groups achieved highest abundance under intermediate fire frequencies. These contrasting responses highlight trade‐offs inherent in fire planning and the importance of considering multiple fire regime components simultaneously. By identifying which elements of the fire regime most strongly drive biodiversity risk, this framework provides a tractable and transferable tool for risk‐based fire planning and conservation prioritization. The use of FRGs and FRSs enables scalable scenario testing and decision support in data‐limited contexts, supporting more transparent, defensible, and adaptive management of biodiversity under changing fire regimes.

items.title: Trapper Citizen Science: An open‐source camera trap platform for citizen science in wildlife research and management
items.abstract: Effective wildlife monitoring is essential for biodiversity conservation and sustainable management, particularly in the face of rapid environmental changes and human–wildlife interactions. Advances in camera trap technology and citizen science, that is, nonprofessional involvement in scientific research, provide noninvasive methods for tracking species distribution, abundance, and behavior across large spatial and temporal scales. However, challenges in managing the vast datasets generated, ensuring user engagement, and addressing privacy concerns persist. To address these issues, we introduce Trapper Citizen Science (Trapper CS), an open‐source platform combining artificial intelligence–based data processing pipelines with citizen science to enhance wildlife monitoring efforts. Trapper CS supports automated data processing, provides user‐friendly interfaces and real‐time species identification, while promoting collaboration and data sharing through standardized protocols and data formats (e.g., Camtrap Data Package). With applications spanning research, management, and citizen engagement, Trapper CS exemplifies a novel approach to integrate technology and public participation for addressing global wildlife challenges. This paper discusses the platform's architecture, functionality, and applications, highlighting its potential to contribute to more effective wildlife monitoring and management.

items.title: Recent trends show a 20 year decline in global biological invasion rates
items.abstract: Biological invasions are costly economically and environmentally. Despite international agreements to mitigate invasions, we have limited understanding of recent trends - the last two decades of invasion records have been typically excluded from analyses, given potential discovery and reporting lags. We use simulations to show discovery lags do not cause spurious recent declines, but reporting lags can do so. Using global empirical patterns, we estimated reporting lags caused up to a 94% underestimation of recent invasion rates. After controlling for these lags, our model estimated that the invasion rate accelerated at 1.5%/yr between 1970 and 2003 up to a maximum of ~650 species/yr, but has since declined to ~150 species/yr in 2020. Thus, for global trends, our analyses indicate that observed empirical declines are likely real and that lags cannot explain them, potentially suggesting that invasion policies have been effective.

items.title: A prediction of the global vertebrate biodiversity exposure to extreme heat under the expected 2026–27 El Niño
items.abstract: Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather, which can be amplified by climatic oscillations such as El Niño. Seasonal forecasts indicate a strong El Niño developing through late 2026 and into 2027, potentially among the largest since records began in 1950, threatening species with temperatures outside the range where they have historically occurred. Here, we showcase how to leverage seasonal climate forecasts and macroecological analysis to provide an early warning system for biodiversity. We combine NASA's GEOS‐S2S seasonal forecasts (May 2026–February 2027) with IUCN range maps and species‐specific thermal thresholds, defined as the 99th percentile of monthly mean temperatures across each species' range over 1980–2024. Working at a monthly resolution, reflecting the highest accuracy of seasonal forecasts, we evaluate sustained heat anomalies. We forecast that 4159 species (17%) will face unprecedented temperatures across > 30% of their range within the forecasting period, including 1870 species of conservation concern. Exposure is expected to be concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere, particularly the Amazon, subtropical Africa, Madagascar and Australia. Heat exposure is predicted to peak in the Southern Hemisphere summer, with January–February 2027 accounting for ca 70% of exposed species. Exposure predictions differed between groups: amphibians (24%) and reptiles (15%), the most heat‐sensitive groups, were disproportionately predicted to be exposed relative to mammals (8%) and birds (6%). Because behavioral buffering might not be sufficient under sustained anomalies, monthly exposure is best interpreted as a signal of sublethal demographic risk, beyond mortality risks that could be characterized at smaller temporal resolutions. Most species predicted to be exposed differ from those predicted to be exposed during the last El Niño. Conservation responses only calibrated to past events may therefore be poorly targeted, highlighting the need for continuous biodiversity forecasting to trigger more effective mitigation and targeted monitoring actions.

items.title: Global assessment of plant naturalizations in habitats
items.abstract: The vulnerability of habitats to plant invasions varies widely, yet habitat identity is often overlooked in large‐scale studies of alien species naturalization. Using the newly developed SynHab database, which links 7250 alien vascular plant species to 14 habitat types across 102 regions worldwide, we assessed the role of different habitats in determining the distribution of naturalized alien plants. We identified which habitats are most vulnerable to invasions by naturalized plants, and how climate, environmental conditions, and human impacts interact with habitat type to determine naturalization levels in world regions. When aggregated into six broad categories, human‐made habitats had the highest number of naturalized species (n = 5483), followed by woody habitats (n = 3463), grasslands (n = 2741), stressful habitats (n = 2741), wetlands (n = 2585), and aquatic habitats (n = 190). These categories varied significantly across continents and zonobiomes in the proportion of naturalized flora harbored, indicating nonrandom global patterns. Species accumulation curves revealed that wetlands, grasslands, and human‐made habitats showed the steepest relative increase in the number of naturalized species with habitat area, whereas aquatic, stressful, and woody habitats exhibited the slowest increases. Key climatic drivers of habitat‐level naturalization included mean annual temperature, maximum temperature of the warmest month and precipitation seasonality, highlighting the importance of heat and drought stress. Human‐related drivers, such as regional per capita GDP or human population density, appeared significant in all habitats but woody and wetlands, and the numbers of naturalized species tended to increase with proxies for propagule pressure and disturbance. Our results show that across present‐day spatial climatic gradients, hot and arid conditions are associated with lower numbers of naturalized alien plants in several habitats. These patterns provide a habitat‐level basis for generating expectations about how plant naturalization may respond to future climate change.

items.title: An iterative subseasonal‐to‐interannual ecological forecast system for Ixodes scapularis, the vector of Lyme disease
items.abstract: Forecasting the population dynamics of disease vectors is critical for mitigating the risks of vector‐borne diseases under a changing climate. We evaluate an iterative Bayesian forecast model of black‐legged tick ( Ixodes scapularis ) phenology and population dynamics at near‐term to interannual (e.g., 12‐month) scales. The black‐legged tick is the vector of Borrelia burgdorferi , the causative agent of human Lyme disease. Our forecasts outperformed a seasonal null model during peak questing periods when disease risk is highest. The null model was based on historical day‐of‐year averages. Iterative data assimilation improved forecast performance over time, demonstrating the ability to adaptively learn about climate‐driven shifts in demographic parameters, and reinforcing the value of long‐term data to support management. Weather and climate variables emerged as the dominant predictors of nymph survival and questing activity, with daily maximum temperature displacing humidity as the strongest predictor as the iterative forecast cycle evolved over time. Short‐term forecasts driven by local weather observations were more accurate than those relying on seasonal climate forecasts, highlighting the importance of fine‐scale weather dynamics and data for subannual predictions. At interannual scales, seasonal climate forecasts and vertebrate host (mouse) abundance were important for maintaining strong predictive skill in forecasting nymphal tick abundance, which is often used as a proxy for risk of human exposure to tick‐borne disease (TBD), but forecasts were largely unaffected by larval abundance. Investment in monitoring efforts should prioritize observations of the nymphal stage to reduce forecast uncertainty. These results offer a path forward for operationalizing ecological forecasts of tick populations under environmental change and underscore the importance of adaptive, process‐based models for managing TBD risk in a changing climate.

items.title: Long‐term camera trapping reveals emerging density‐dependent dynamics in a recovering apex predator
items.abstract: Effective management of recovering large carnivores depends on monitoring systems that are accurate, scalable, and cost‐efficient. This need is particularly acute in Europe, where rapid wolf recolonization is creating new challenges for management and policy. Individual identification, on which conventional monitoring often relies, can be costly and logistically demanding, but for social carnivores the reproductive unit can be a more practical and management‐relevant target. Building on this, we conducted systematic winter camera trap surveys between 2015 and 2023 at 102 fixed sites in the Western Swiss Alps and characterized gray wolf recolonization dynamics without individual identifications. By combining group detections with a spatial clustering algorithm, we delineated putative wolf packs and tracked their expansion over time. These packs then served as detection units in a spatial capture–recapture model to estimate pack density in 2022/2023. Wolves progressively recolonized the Valais Alps south of the Rhône River, with wolf detections at 50% of camera sites and group detections at 30%. By 2022/2023, we identified 10 packs, some transboundary with Italy and France, with a mean detected group size of 2.9 individuals and at least 31 wolves in reproductive units. We estimated 0.4 packs/100 km 2 and a distribution that aligned well with extant reference maps. Population growth indices increased strongly over time: Exponential models best described growth of overall trapping rates (TRs) and minimum number of individuals and packs, while logistic models provided better fits for naïve occupancy and pack‐specific TRs. Our findings show that wolf recovery has recently shifted from early exponential growth to a more regulated phase of density‐dependent dynamics. This transition, corresponding to peak population growth, occurred 1 year prior to the initiation of intensive, proactive wolf regulation in Switzerland in December 2023. At this stage of recovery, reducing population size through lethal control requires sustained high offtake and poses substantial management challenges. Under the conditions of our study system, camera trapping combined with spatial clustering characterized population recovery cost‐effectively and could contribute to coordinated monitoring programs in an increasingly connected European carnivore landscape. To assess cold adaptation, we quantified cold tolerance and its physiological and biochemical basis through common‐garden experiments across six populations spanning the species' latitudinal invasion gradient. Additionally, we examined epigenetic regulation of cold adaptation by assessing expression and DNA methylation of the AcICE1 gene, measured lifespan and reproductive traits (number of capitula and fruits) under simulated frost conditions and monitored lifespan under natural field conditions. Ageratum conyzoides expanded progressively from tropical and subtropical into temperate China, accompanied by an unexpected decline in cold tolerance during its 109‐year invasion. This shift towards enhanced cold sensitivity was associated with downregulation of the cold‐response transcription factor AcICE1 and lower full‐length methylation of the AcICE1 gene. Under simulated frost, northern populations had shorter lifespans and showed a greater capacity to complete reproduction under progressive cooling, whereas reproductive performance was more strongly reduced in southern populations. Synthesis . This study reveals a counterintuitive pattern during the poleward expansion of A. conyzoides : rather than evolving enhanced cold tolerance, the species exhibited increased cold sensitivity. This enhanced cold sensitivity co‐occurred with life cycle acceleration in northern populations, and this trait combination represents an integrated freeze‐avoidance strategy that facilitates successful expansion towards higher latitudes. These findings provide a new perspective on how invasive annual herbs successfully avoid freezing temperatures during poleward range expansion.

items.title: Syndromes of multidimensional beta diversity change in invaded metacommunities
items.abstract: NeoBiota 110: 163-191 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.110.171934 Authors: William K. Annis, Lily M. Thompson, Luke M. Bower, Stephen R. Midway, Julian D. Olden, Brandon K. Peoples Abstract: Beta diversity change Δβ caused by nonnative species introductions is multifaceted (taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic) and is comprised of three components (total beta diversity, replacement, and richness difference). As such, community change due to species invasions represents a nine-dimensional phenomenon. These complementary dimensions can be simplified by delineating Δβ syndromes—groups of local communities within a broader metacommunity that experience correlated changes in the nine diversity dimensions due to nonnative species occurrences. We introduce the concept of Δβ syndromes to provide insight into invasion-driven community reassembly and identify scenarios in which nonnative species cause community changes that are not detectable in single dimensions (e.g., taxonomic Δβ). Using 1,023 stream fish communities across the conterminous United States, we quantified community-level Δβ using changes in nine dimensions of local contribution to beta diversity (ΔLCBD)—the distinctness of a community’s composition relative to all others across the metacommunity. We calculated null model standardized effect sizes for each ΔLCBD value, and retained the 437 communities that had a statistically significant ΔLCBD effect size in at least one dimension. We then used model-based clustering them into syndromes based on correlated changes in the nine dimensions of ΔLCBD effect sizes. We identified six Δβ syndromes that differed in magnitude and direction of multidimensional Δβ. No syndromes were characterized by communities that contributed to homogenization in each of the three diversity facets, illustrating that taxonomic Δβ alone is insufficient to understand the consequences of invasions. Syndromes also differed in native and nonnative species compositions; these communities’ contributions to Δβ reflect a combination of historical biogeography and contemporary invasion processes. Notably, some syndromes represented communities that did not contain any nonnative species; instead, these sites’ contributions to Δβ resulted from nonnative species occurrences in other communities reshaping the broader metacommunity structure around uninvaded communities. The Δβ syndrome framework can shed light on the local- and metacommunity-level effects of nonnative species establishment that traditional taxonomic approaches may overlook and provide insights into the processes that facilitate these effects. items.title: Biodiversity and ecosystem services in changing landscapes: a biome level scenario assessment for continental Ecuador
items.abstract: Context Ecuador hosts remarkable biogeographical areas, including the Coast, the Andes and the Amazon, which represent distinctive biomes. However, a comprehensive assessment accounting for biome-specific differences in the landscape as well as in biodiversity and ecosystem services (BES) across Ecuador is still lacking. Additionally, the experts were involved in developing simulation conditions for the scenarios, which were applied in the spatially explicit modeling platform based on Geographic Information System and Cellular Automaton modules. Results The scenario impacts were visualized as changes in landscape configuration and BES capacities at the biome level. Regarding the deforestation scenarios, the Amazon biome showed the most notable change, with 11–13% of loss in most BES except food provision. However, the BES of the Andean biome presented the most evident trade-offs between BES by the afforestation scenarios with an approximately 10% decrease in food provision, while there was a 20–30% increase in other BES. BES capacity maps for all three biomes clearly showed that BES hotspots were reduced by the deforestation scenarios, whereas the afforestation scenarios expanded BES hotspots. Conclusions Experts’ feedback on the applied methods and the results confirmed the usefulness of the BES assessment for future landscape management with further consideration of how to transfer the findings into policy-related information.

items.title: Surviving the Antarctic: thermal tolerance adjustment in an invasive population of Psychoda albipennis (Zetterstedt, 1850)
items.abstract: Biological invasions in polar ecosystems are an increasing concern under climate change and intensifying human activity. We compared two geographically distant populations of the invasive dipteran Psychoda albipennis (Maritime Antarctica and the Magellanic sub-Antarctic) to assess population-level variation in lower and upper thermal tolerance. We further contextualized these responses through an exploratory comparison with published thermal-tolerance data for the non-native Trichocera maculipennis and the native Parochlus steinenii . Thermal responses in P. albipennis were asymmetric: responses to cooling were largely conserved between populations, whereas upper thermal tolerance diverged markedly, with the Antarctic population exhibiting a higher CT max and a slower decline in activity as temperature increased. In the exploratory interspecific comparison, all three species showed broadly similar responses to cooling, whereas P. albipennis and T. maculipennis exhibited higher upper thermal thresholds than P. steinenii . Together, these findings identify upper thermal tolerance as the primary axis of phenotypic thermal differentiation between P. albipennis populations. The broader functional thermal breadth observed in the Antarctic population may enhance persistence under thermally variable conditions, although the relative contributions of phenotypic plasticity, environmental filtering, and heritable evolutionary change remain unresolved.

items.title: When does modelling dependence change the interpretation of biodiversity indicators?
items.abstract: Recent biodiversity trend analyses have modelled uncertainty arising from temporal, spatial and phylogenetic dependence. For primarily descriptive indicators such as the Living Planet Indices (LPIs) however, a prior question is whether dependence modelling improves estimation of a fixed quantity or actually changes the quantity being reported. Using the high‐profile case of Johnson et al., the current paper argues that covariance‐rich hierarchical models can make the relationship between a reported model coefficient and an intended estimand ambiguous. When aggregate trends are estimated from common coefficients in latent models with structured covariance, observations contribute unequal independent information to the estimator through assumed redundancy among related units. The reported collective trend is then a model‐based coefficient (e.g. a mean over a latent‐effect distribution) shaped by partial pooling and dependence; this is not automatically an average under declared estimand or ‘aggregation’ weights that indicator trend users may assume. A further ambiguity is whether the reported coefficient summarises the analysed sample or supports claims about a broader spatial, taxonomic or other policy‐relevant domain. One defensible reply, that the model is merely a more efficient estimator of a sample average, requires explicit statement of the estimand, weighting scheme, relationship between the model output and that estimand, and evidence of performance for that target; predictive success alone is not sufficient for this descriptive claim. Claims concerning broader generalisability require accompanying risk‐of‐bias assessments where evaluation against the true target (e.g. a time trend in some facet of global biodiversity) is unobtainable. The implication is that covariance‐rich hierarchical indicator analyses should state the estimand, the role of dependence modelling, missing data assumptions and domain of inference clearly before interpreting the resulting trend for scientific or policy applications.

items.title: Bird ringing data reveals country‐wide spatial and temporal patterns in mortality from window collisions
items.abstract: Urbanization poses various threats to bird populations worldwide, of which bird‐window collisions (BWCs) contribute to a significant proportion of human‐related bird mortalities. We observed BWCs in almost half of all breeding bird species in Finland, with species‐specific collision risks being significantly associated with habitat preferences. Species favouring urban and forested areas were more likely to collide than species utilizing open and aquatic habitats. First‐year birds collided at higher rates than adults, following distinct seasonal patterns in collision occurrences, with collision rates (i.e. adjusted for species abundances) peaking during winter and collision frequencies peaking during the migration seasons. Our results highlight an urgent need for monitoring and risk prediction tools for mitigation efforts on BWCs, particularly for high‐risk species and in rural areas. Given the wide availability of standardized ringing and recovery data with extensive spatiotemporal and taxonomic coverage, our approach highlights strong potential for novel applications in the prioritization of BWC mitigation efforts across broad spatiotemporal domains, offering a valuable complement to traditional field survey data

items.title: Will they survive? The critical status of Asiatic cheetahs in Iran
items.abstract: The Asiatic cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus venaticus), once widespread, now survives only in Iran, with its population nearing extinction. Using extensive camera trap surveys across eight reserves, supplemented by published records of cheetah occurrences on social media, we identified 24 adult cheetahs in the Northern and Southern Landscapes. No reproduction or new individuals have been recorded in the Southern Landscape for over a decade, while the Northern Landscape supports the remaining population, likely fewer than 30 adult individuals. From 2012 to 2024, at least 38 cubs were born from eight females in the Northern Landscape, with 74.1% surviving their first year. Camera traps enabled us to effectively identify individuals but are limited for tracking fine-scale movements, underscoring the need for satellite telemetry. Roadside fencing, wildlife underpasses, habitat protection, community-based land management, and stronger anti-trafficking measures are critical to enhance survival. items.title: Drivers of alien plant invasion levels depend on the invasion stage and residence time
items.abstract: Alien plant invasion levels are influenced by various environmental and anthropogenic factors, as well as by the characteristics of recipient native communities. Two contrasting hypotheses—environmental filtering and limiting similarity—predict the success of alien species based on their phylogenetic and functional (dis)similarity to native species. However, their effects on invasion levels across different invasion stages and residence times remain poorly understood. We hypothesize that greater similarity between native and alien species (environmental filtering) increases invasion levels, particularly during the naturalization stage, whereas lower similarity between native and alien species (limiting similarity) increases invasion levels, particularly during the invasion stage. We analysed invasion levels, defined as the proportions of naturalized and invasive species (further subdivided into archaeophytes and neophytes), in 2368 grid cells across the Czech Republic. For each cell, we quantified phylogenetic relatedness and functional similarity between resident native species and the national alien species pool to estimate the availability of suitable (preadapted) alien species that could invade the cell. Using spatial simultaneous autoregressive error models, we related invasion levels to these variables, as well as to environmental, anthropogenic and landscape factors. Phylogenetic relatedness had a strong positive effect on invasion levels across all species groups, regardless of residence time or invasion stage. Functional similarity showed the same pattern for naturalized species and naturalized archaeophytes but negatively affected the levels of invasion by invasive species. Invasive species and naturalized neophytes were more strongly influenced by environmental and anthropogenic factors, particularly by the extent of urbanized areas. Overall, invasion levels were higher in fragmented landscapes and lower in semi‐natural forested landscapes. Synthesis . Drivers of alien plant invasion levels vary with invasion stage and residence time. The strong positive effects of phylogenetic relatedness and functional similarity to native species on the levels of invasion by naturalized species, particularly those present in the country for a long time, support the importance of environmental filtering at this stage. Conversely, reduced functional similarity and the strong effects of climate on invasive species suggest that their increased invasion levels may be associated with niche segregation from native species in favourable environments.

items.title: Distance from the climatic niche optimum explains climate‐change‐driven dynamics in Mediterranean shrublands

items.title: Partitioning the variance of species–area relation into sampling‐ versus scale‐dependent components
items.abstract: The species–area relation (SAR) has been extensively studied over the past century, yet the sources of variation around an estimated SAR curve remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the sampling variance of the SAR can be decomposed into two additive components: 1) conditional variance, assuming that regional richness is fixed and represents uncertainty associated with local sampling; and 2) an additional component attributable to uncertainty in regional species richness, including uncertainty arising from rare species that remain undetected in the regional sample. We establish this decomposition mathematically and evaluate its behavior through numerical simulations. On this basis, empirical SAR observations can be classified as falling within the conditional confidence interval (CI), within the gap between the conditional and unconditional CIs, or outside the unconditional CI. The last outcome indicates variation not accounted for by the two sampling‐dependent components and may reflect scale‐dependent ecological processes or other sources of unexplained variation. Empirical applications showed that the relative contributions of local sampling uncertainty, regional richness uncertainty, and variation beyond these sampling‐dependent components differed among datasets, spatial scales, and sampling designs. For spatially explicit sampling of a tropical forest plot stem‐mapping dataset, observations were generally consistent with local sampling uncertainty when small sampling grains were freely distributed across space. In contrast, observations from a single contiguous sampling area more frequently fell outside the unconditional CI, a pattern that may reflect spatially structured ecological processes not represented by the sampling‐variance components. For nested sampling of amphibian diversity on the Chengdu Plain in SW China, both local sampling uncertainty and variation beyond the unconditional CI were frequently observed, whereas uncertainty in regional richness became more prominent when the local sampling area fraction exceeded 0.6. The resulting classifications also varied with the order of nested sampling: for the amphibian dataset, the large‐to‐small scheme accumulated species richness more slowly than the small‐to‐large scheme did. In conclusion, we develop a novel and readily applicable hierarchical variance‐partitioning framework to distinguish variation attributable to local sampling, uncertainty in regional richness, and variation not explained by these sampling‐dependent components along SAR curves.

Location Global scale Time period 2000-2019 Major taxa studied Given their exceptional diversity and climatic sensitivity, insects provide a powerful system for studying these responses. items.title: Spatial conservation planning influences coral adaptive potential
items.abstract: The adaptive capacity of reefs to survive ocean warming and local stressors is driven by ecological and evolutionary processes occurring at multiple spatial scales. items.title: Climate Change and Habitat Loss Threaten Taxonomic and Functional Diversity of Endemic Primates in South America

Taxonomic diversity was estimated as species richness, whereas functional diversity was quantified as mean pairwise distance (MPD), which represents the average functional dissimilarity among co‐occurring taxa based on body mass, activity pattern, habitat, and trophic guild, at a 5 km resolution. items.title: deepSTRAPP: An R package to assess trait‐ and range‐dependent diversification dynamics over time
items.abstract: Understanding how diversification dynamics interact with species traits and geographical distributions over time remains a central challenge in macroevolution and biogeography. Yet the timing of these associations is rarely tested explicitly: existing approaches often focus on present‐day trait–rate relationships, or summarize over the whole history of a clade, overlooking variations in historical processes acting over deep evolutionary timescales. We introduce deepSTRAPP , an R package for assessing trait‐ and range‐dependent diversification across any temporal interval. deepSTRAPP models the evolution of traits or ranges independently of diversification rates on time‐calibrated phylogenies, extracts inferred values at user‐defined time steps and performs semi‐parametric STRAPP (Structured Rate Permutations on Phylogenies) tests based on block‐permutation to identify time windows in which diversification rates varied with species attributes. It handles continuous, categorical and biogeographic data, and includes visualization tools to explore the evolution of traits, ranges, diversification rates and the significance of their associations through time. Applied to empirical datasets, deepSTRAPP provided critical new perspectives to macroevolutionary questions inaccessible to currently available methods. It uncovered significant state‐dependent dynamics confined to restricted time windows that whole‐tree analyses overlooked, and tempered conclusions about present‐day associations that did not extend substantially back through evolutionary time. By explicitly testing for temporal variation in trait‐ and range‐dependent diversification, deepSTRAPP provides a robust framework to disentangle the relative contributions of past versus recent processes in shaping biodiversity patterns across broad phylogenetic and temporal scales.

items.title: The Filtering Effects of Urban Environments on Frugivorous Birds Worldwide

items.title: Blueprints for restoration: Molecular monitoring and remote sensing support dispersal‐driven kelp recolonization
items.abstract: Nearshore marine habitats generate services worth billions of dollars, yet they are undergoing rapid, widespread degradation worldwide. Connectivity to extant kelp in 2023 was a significant predictor of gametophyte density, kelp canopy occurrence, and habitat recolonization in 2024, suggesting that dispersal plays an important role in recolonization. By linking spatial connectivity with densities of microscopic life stages and recolonization, this work offers valuable guidance for designing and implementing effective kelp restoration strategies.

items.title: Complex lake effects structure bryophyte communities across spatial scales around Lake Superior, Canada
items.abstract: Context Studies have found that large lakes significantly modify regional climates, an influence known as the “lake effect”. Large lakes may provide biodiversity refugia in a changing climate owing to the lake effect, but the impacts of lake effects on biodiversity remain poorly documented. Methods We sampled bryophyte communities on three substrates (trees, rocks, and logs) across 54 sites on and near the northern and eastern shores of Lake Superior. We combined community data with climate and forest data to determine the influence of variables at each of three spatial scales—micro (forest attributes), meso (lake effect), and macro (regional climatic norms)—on community composition and richness. Results The lake effect structured community composition, along with regional climate norms and forest characteristics. The lake effect was divided into three orthogonal axes. Notably, each of these axes included a distinct component of the moisture environment—precipitation, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit—and our results suggest that these components have divergent effects on bryophyte communities. The lake effect had no significant influence on species richness. Conclusions Lake Superior induces biotically important climatic heterogeneity that structures bryophyte communities across the study region. items.title: Climate change drives northward range shifts in invasive forest pests and pathogens
items.abstract: Invasive tree pests and pathogens are increasingly threatening forests worldwide. items.title: Protected Areas Reduce Heat Exposure in Squamates Globally
items.abstract: Protected areas (PAs) are central to biodiversity conservation, yet their capacity to buffer species from climate‐driven heat exposure, that is, the duration and frequency of exposure to temperatures exceeding species' critical thermal limits, remains poorly quantified at global scales. items.title: Climate‐driven compositional shifts across a temperate–subtropical island ecotone
items.abstract: Climate change is expected to drive substantial shifts in species distributions, yet ecological responses are often delayed under disequilibrium dynamics, limiting the effectiveness of range‐based indicators for detecting ongoing change. Using a comprehensive dataset of island floras across a temperate–subtropical transition in South Korea, we quantify temporal changes in the relative representation of warm‐temperate and subtropical plant (WTSP) assemblages. By emphasizing proportional changes along latitudinal gradients, we detect directional redistribution within communities even in the absence of pronounced changes in gradient shape. Our results reveal patterns consistent with northward redistribution of WTSP composition across survey periods, despite minimal changes in overall gradient form, indicating that community‐level redistribution can occur prior to detectable range shifts or richness changes. These findings highlight the sensitivity of cumulative, direction‐sensitive compositional metrics for detecting early ecological responses to climate warming. More broadly, this study provides a generalizable framework for detecting compositional redistribution through cumulative inference, even when conventional approaches may have limited sensitivity under some conditions, and for identifying early signals of climate‐driven change across gradient‐structured ecological systems. items.title: Migrant frugivorous birds assist plants in tracking climate change: A first spatially explicit approach
items.abstract: Climate change is causing biodiversity redistributions towards cooler areas at an unprecedented velocity. Plants are an essential component of terrestrial ecosystems that primarily rely on seed dispersal to redistribute. Yet, most seed dispersal occurs over short distances (i.e. less than 1 km), which is insufficient to track ongoing climate change. Bird migration can support seed dispersal at longer distances. However, we lack spatially explicit estimations of seed dispersal by migratory birds towards future climatically suitable ranges of plants. Thereby, it remains unclear to what extent they can facilitate plant redistribution in the coming decades. We integrated spatially explicit, seed‐dispersal models with projections on plant climatic suitability using species distribution models. We simulated long‐distance dispersal of 14 fleshy‐fruited plant species across Europe during the northward spring migration of song thrushes ( Turdus philomelos ), an adequate model species given its abundance, migratory behaviour and key role as disperser of native European plants. Dispersal models were replicated under three global warming projections and three scenarios of dispersal sensitivity to land‐cover alteration. Plant climatically suitable ranges will shift northwards by 248–948 km under severe warming projections by the year 2090. We identified a strong negative effect of warmer climate projections and higher dispersal sensitivity to land‐cover alteration on seed‐dispersal range filling (i.e. the proportion of future climatically suitable area that is currently unsuitable and receives seed‐dispersal events). items.title: Priority–green island synergy: A testable hypothesis for insect-mediated invasional facilitation in Eucalyptus plantations
items.abstract: NeoBiota 110: 113-121 DOI: 10.3897/neobiota.110.207941 Authors: Xiu Xu, Zhende Yang Abstract: Non-native forest plantations can concentrate susceptible hosts, recurrently receive alien organisms through movements of planting material and thereby become focal points for biological invasions. Yet, whether an alien insect can directly alter host tissues in ways that facilitate a later alien insect remains poorly understood. We propose priority–green island synergy as a testable hypothesis for insect-mediated invasional facilitation. In southern China, the earlier-detected gall inducer Leptocybe invasa and the later-detected leaf gallers Ophelimus bipolaris and O. maskelli provide a candidate system. Leptocybe invasa galls alter nutrient, phenolic and phytohormone profiles and may generate transient physiological islands in galled or connected tissues. The hypothesis predicts that, after host genotype, tissue age, microclimate and propagule pressure are controlled, prior L. invasa attack should increase Ophelimus host acceptance, gall initiation or survival; that any benefit should co-vary with measurable physiological traits; that locally mediated effects should decline with increasing distance from the primary L. invasa gall; that the direction and magnitude of the response should vary with primary gall density and the interval between primary and secondary attack; and that any facilitative response should co-vary with realised gall development and associated physiological changes. Taken together, these predictions are designed to distinguish gall-mediated facilitation from alternative explanations for co-occurrence, including shared host susceptibility, propagule pressure, environmental filtering and variation in local adult abundance. We outline matched field surveys, controlled arrival-order experiments and physiological mediation tests that can evaluate the hypothesis and distinguish facilitation from alternative explanations. If supported, priority–green island synergy would show how an alien insect can engineer host tissues in ways that increase plantation invasibility. If unsupported, the same tests will delimit when plant-mediated interactions amongst alien herbivores are neutral or antagonistic rather than facilitative. HTML XML PDF

items.title: Assessing the accuracy and stability of variable importance in species distribution modelling algorithms through sample perturbations
items.abstract: Variable importance derived from species distribution modelling (SDM) is widely used to identify key environmental drivers of species distributions. However, the reliability of these inferences has rarely been systematically evaluated, particularly with respect to their sensitivity to individual occurrences. Here, we used virtual species and developed a sample perturbations diagnostic framework, in which each occurrence was systematically removed (leave‐one‐out) to assess how small changes in the input data affect variable importance inference. Using this framework, we evaluated and compared ten SDM algorithms across multiple scenarios. We constructed a set of evaluation metrics to quantify both the accuracy of driver identification and the stability of permutation importance estimates, defined as their variability under sample perturbations. We further investigated the sample level mechanisms underlying instability. Our results showed that random forest (RF), gradient boosting machine (GBM), and maximum entropy (Maxent) achieved the best overall performance. RF exhibited the relatively high inferential accuracy and stability, but showed limited ability to differentiate the relative importance of environmental variables. GBM and Maxent achieved slightly lower accuracy than RF, but were more stable and effective for distinguishing the relative contributions of different variables. Instead, several algorithms displayed relatively high accuracy but were sensitive to sample perturbations. Scenario analyses indicated that stability generally increased under conditions of high sample sizes, low geographical sampling bias, and moderate prevalence. Highly influential occurrences were not necessarily associated with extreme environmental conditions. Removal experiments further demonstrated that variable importance inference in several algorithms was sensitive to a relatively small subset of occurrences, highlighting the disproportionate contribution of these occurrences. Overall, this study provides a sample level diagnostic framework for evaluating the reliability of variable importance in SDM, offering practical guidance for improving the interpretability of environmental driver inference in ecological research and conservation applications.

items.title: Hunters in Danger: Evolutionary Diversity and Conservation Priorities in Carnivore Species of the American Continent
items.abstract: Aim Many mammals of the order Carnivora are key ecosystem predators. In the American continent, they have a complex biogeographical history, shaped by processes of colonization and adaptive radiation that have generated a high diversity of lineages. However, under the global biodiversity crisis, this group faces increasing extinction risk, and conservation efforts have focused mainly on species richness while neglecting evolutionary relationships. We aimed to assess the distribution of evolutionary diversity in carnivores of the American continent and its relationship with biological and geographical variables to recognize species and areas with unique evolutionary value. Location American continent. Methods We evaluated 104 carnivore species of the Americas. Using data from public literature, we calculated Evolutionary Distinctiveness (ED), Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered (EDGE; EDGE2), and Biogeographically weighted Evolutionary Distinctiveness (BED) metrics. In addition, we explored the relationship between evolutionary scores with body size, altitudinal and latitudinal distribution of species, and mapped spatial patterns of richness and evolutionary metrics to identify priority areas for conservation. Results The evolutionary diversity of carnivores was unevenly distributed across regions and taxonomic groups. In terrestrial species, all evolutionary scores decreased with altitude, and only ED followed a unimodal pattern with latitude, concentrating in the tropical belt; in marine species, ED clustered in the temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere. A positive relationship was detected between body size and ED in marine species, and a negative relationship was observed with BED in terrestrial species and across all carnivores. Spatial patterns of richness were consistent with those of ED, EDGE and EDGE2 scores, but differed from those obtained with BED scores. Main Conclusion Our findings demonstrate the importance of incorporating evolutionary metrics into the prioritization of American carnivores as a means to safeguard their evolutionary history and to optimize conservation planning and resource allocation from a comprehensive perspective.

items.title: Metabolic ecology and habitat stability explain the disproportionately high species richness in standing waters
items.abstract: The metabolic theory of ecology (MTE) conceptualizes that temperature is the primary driver of species richness, a pattern well supported in terrestrial taxa but less certain for freshwater organisms. Limited global‐scale evidence and frequent violations of MTE's assumptions, particularly regarding the stationarity of body size and abundance, further undermine its applicability. In freshwater systems, body size and abundance are tightly linked to dispersal and range size, which differ markedly between running‐water (lotic) and standing‐water (lentic) species, as proposed by the Habitat‐Stability–Dispersal Hypothesis (HSDH). Adaptations to habitat stability may therefore generate distinct biogeographical patterns of traits and modify richness–temperature relationships predicted by MTE. Utilizing comprehensive global functional, phylogenetic, and distributional data on dragonfly and damselfly species (83%) and habitat information (46%), we tested MTE predictions for lentic versus lotic species. Lotic species richness followed MTE expectations (slope: −0.469) more closely than lentic species richness (slope: −0.283). The proportion of lentic species in an assemblage was the strongest predictor of deviation in the species richness–temperature relationship ( R 2 = 38%). Assemblages dominated by lentic species clustered in climatically unstable regions and mainly included smaller‐bodied species with larger ranges. Phylogenetic comparative analysis shows a strong phylogenetic signal in habitat preference, with the most species‐rich and northerly distributed families comprising predominantly lentic species. Our findings suggest that adaptations to habitat stability facilitated the colonization and persistence of lentic species in harsh and fluctuating climates, both past and present, resulting in largely divergent species richness patterns of lentic and lotic odonates. Integrating HSDH‐related traits (body and range size) not only substantially improves the explanatory power of the MTE but also reveals a trait syndrome with broad implications for the biogeography and climate change responses of freshwater communities.

items.title: From patterns to predictions: a framework for the spatial epidemiology of wildlife diseases
items.abstract: Wildlife diseases pose a significant threat to biodiversity conservation, public health, and livestock. Spatial epidemiology provides a robust framework to understand disease dynamics and guide policy and management. However, the rapid proliferation of spatial methods has largely occurred in isolation across disciplines, leaving the field without a unified framework that connects these approaches and clarifies their strengths, limitations, and applications. The spatial epidemiology workflow includes three main steps: 1) descriptive analysis of spatial patterns; 2) exploration of observed patterns through explicative analyses; and 3) prediction of pathogen distribution and spread. Descriptive analysis, such as disease mapping and clustering analysis, identifies spatial patterns and informs hypotheses about potential risk factors. Subsequently, explicative analyses can link pathogen presence to ecological or anthropogenic drivers and explain spatiotemporal dynamics. Drivers of pathogen transmission can be further understood through mechanistic models, ranging from population‐level Susceptible‐Infected‐Removed (SIR) frameworks to individual‐ or group‐based SIR approaches such as metapopulation and network models that can incorporate host behavior and social structure. Molecular epidemiology, through genetic variant identification and phylogenetic mapping, can identify outbreak origins and host linkages. Lastly, predictions of pathogen distribution and spread are enabled by ecological niche models and species distribution models, which project potential pathogen distributions based on ecological, geographical, and/or anthropogenic factors, and by mechanistic simulations that parameterize pathogen spread processes to predict expansion over space and time. System‐based simulations focus on population‐level dynamics, while agent‐based simulations incorporate individual‐level dynamics, offering detailed insights into pathogen spread and control measures. Consequently, the integration of descriptive analyses, explicative procedures, and predictive models provides a robust framework for addressing the challenges posed by wildlife diseases and developing management and control measures.

items.title: Human pressure, habitat heterogeneity and species traits jointly determine the level of dark diversity in coastal fish communities
items.abstract: Understanding how anthropogenic pressures and environmental gradients shape coastal fish communities is a central question in biogeography and marine conservation. Yet, the set of species expected to occur at a site given ecological conditions but being absent – the so‐called dark diversity – has received far less attention than observed species, even if they hold key information about local extirpations and conservation effectiveness. Quantifying dark diversity in the sea is particularly challenging because many species are rare, cryptobenthic or mobile, while sampling effort is rarely standardized. Here we combined 930 environmental DNA (eDNA) samples collected at 401 sites along 2000 km of the French Mediterranean coast with fine‐scale mapping of habitats, anthropogenic pressures and protection levels. Using a Bayesian model of dark diversity affinity (DDA) that explicitly controls for sampling effort, we decomposed the correlates of species absences into site characteristics and species traits, separating dispersal‐related from sensitivity‐related signals. At the site level, fishing effort, marine traffic, and artificial habitats were associated with greater DDA, so a deficit of species, whereas protected areas and diverse natural habitats were associated with lower DDA, increasing the likelihood of observing more complete fish communities. At the species level, demersal and predator species, together with those bearing their eggs (e.g. many elasmobranchs) compared to species with demersal or pelagic eggs, exhibited the highest DDA, suggesting local extirpations linked to a combination of limited dispersal and higher sensitivity to cumulative pressures. Beyond the creation of marine protected areas, preserving habitat heterogeneity and mitigating coastal pressures therefore emerge as essential levers to limit the local erosion of fish biodiversity. More broadly, coupling eDNA with a sampling‐effort‐corrected DDA framework offers a transferable benchmark to evaluate where, and for which species, conservation efforts are most needed.

items.title: ZonationR: An R interface to the Zonation software for reproducible spatial conservation prioritisation workflows
items.abstract: Systematic conservation planning provides a science‐based framework for defining conservation goals and supporting transparent spatial decision‐making under limited resources. Within this framework, spatial conservation prioritisation tools are widely used to identify areas of high biodiversity value by integrating information on species distributions, connectivity, costs, and other factors into spatially explicit recommendations. ‘Zonation' is one of the leading software tools in this field, producing hierarchical priority rankings of landscapes based on conservation value. However, its standard workflow typically relies on manual steps for data preparation, execution, and post‐processing, which can become inefficient and difficult to reproduce when multiple scenarios are analysed, limiting accessibility and broader uptake. We introduce ‘ZonationR', an R package that provides a streamlined interface to the ‘Zonation' software, enabling fully reproducible and automated spatial prioritisation workflows. The package integrates the entire analysis pipeline, encompassing input preparation, execution of ‘Zonation', and post‐processing, while supporting both single‐variant and multi‐variant workflows. ‘ZonationR' also provides tools to explore and interpret outputs, including priority maps, feature performance curves, cost summaries, feature representation metrics, and similarity assessments between prioritisation solutions. By linking directly to the original ‘Zonation' engine, the package enables users to benefit from ongoing methodological developments in ‘Zonation' and access its functionality through a transparent, script‐based workflow, thereby reducing technical barriers to running and understanding spatial prioritisation analyses. Beyond these advantages, its integration within the R environment supports iterative testing of conservation scenarios and more rigorous assessment of methodological decisions, while facilitating seamless connections with wider ecological workflows (e.g. species distribution modelling). As conservation planning increasingly relies on large, complex, multi‐source datasets and integrative approaches, such integration is essential for enabling robust, transparent, and reproducible decision‐making across spatial scales.

items.title: Predicting Red List categories reveals hidden extinction risk in one of the world’s most diverse freshwater invertebrate families
items.abstract: Global Red List assessments suggest that approximately 25% of freshwater animal species are at risk of extinction. However, these estimates remain tentative due to insufficient assessments of numerous species-rich invertebrate groups in neglected ecosystems, such as springs and subterranean waters. Including these overlooked taxa in extinction risk assessments is crucial for conservation. To address this gap, we predicted extinction risk in Hydrobiidae, the most diverse family of freshwater gastropods. We compiled occurrence, environmental, and trait data for 876 hydrobiid species and employed deep-learning models trained on International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List assessments to predict extinction risk for 403 Data Deficient and Not Evaluated species. We further analyzed the relative importance and effect of geographic, environmental, and biological predictors and compared extinction risk across habitats, ecoregions, and subfamily clades. Predictive models indicated that extinction risk within Hydrobiidae is underestimated; incorporating predicted assessments suggests that over 60% of species may be threatened. Geographic range attributes, particularly area of occupancy, were the strongest predictors of extinction risk, followed by climate and habitat. Threatened species are concentrated in springs and lakes, and in several freshwater ecoregions of the Mediterranean Basin, North Africa, and western North America. Hydrobiidae exceed most plant and vertebrate groups in both the proportion of endangered evolutionary history and the number of Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered (EDGE) species. Our findings demonstrate that predictive assessments can substantially expand Red List coverage and reveal overlooked patterns of extinction risk across understudied taxa, particularly freshwater invertebrates.
